summary: Provides the RESTCONF binding for dynamic subscriptions, covering both subscribed notifications and YANG-Push. It explains how a RESTCONF client establishes and manages subscriptions to event streams and datastore updates over HTTP.

plainLanguage.summary: This explains how to sign up for live updates from a network device using web-style requests, called RESTCONF.

questions: how does yang push work over restconf
how to subscribe to notifications over restconf
subtitle: How a client asks a network device for a live feed of events and data changes using plain HTTP requests.

tldr.problem: RFC 8639 and RFC 8641 define dynamic subscriptions to YANG events and datastore updates, but not how to carry them over RESTCONF, the HTTP-based management protocol.
tldr.mechanism: The subscriber sends a RESTCONF POST to run the establish-subscription RPC, gets back a subscription ID and a URI, then sends an HTTP GET to that URI so the publisher streams notification messages back as Server-Sent Events.
tldr.outcome: It adds one leaf, uri, to three places in the subscription model, and fixes the error codes, QoS handling and access rules for RESTCONF. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: New data node
facts.value: One leaf, uri, augmented into 3 places

today: RFC 8650 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2019. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What This Document Adds
sections.content:
RFC 8639 defines mechanisms for event subscription, and RFC 8641 adds YANG datastore subscription and YANG-Push. Neither says how to carry a subscription over a particular transport. RFC 8650 is that transport specification for dynamic subscriptions over RESTCONF (RFC 8040). The requirements behind the mechanisms are captured in RFC 7923.

The streaming of the notifications themselves uses the mechanism in Section 6.3 of RFC 8040. The terms subscriber, publisher, receiver, event stream and notification message are taken from RFC 8639.
sections.plainLanguage: Other documents say what a subscription is. This one says how to ask for one using ordinary web requests.

sections.title: Setting Up a Subscription: POST, then GET
sections.content:
Subscribing to event streams uses the RPCs from RFC 8639, Section 2.4, sent as RESTCONF POST requests. Datastore subscription works through the augmentations described in RFC 8641.

A subscriber cannot know the URI of a subscription in advance, because it only exists after the establish-subscription RPC has been accepted. So the POST takes the place of the GET that RFC 8040 would use to discover the URI. The response carries both a subscription ID and a URI. The subscriber then sends a GET to that URI to start the flow of notification messages. Per RFC 8639, the subscription does not become active until that GET is received.

The notifications come back as Server-Sent Events (SSE) in the response to the GET. Two connections are involved: (a) carries the RPC requests and (b) carries the GET and the resulting stream. Each can be a TCP connection or an HTTP/2 stream. RESTCONF servers SHOULD NOT send the SSE event or id fields.

There cannot be two simultaneous GET requests on one subscription URI. A second GET while one is current MUST be rejected with HTTP error code 409.
sections.plainLanguage: First you fill in a sign-up form (the POST) and get a ticket with a special address. Then you go to that address (the GET), and the news starts to arrive.

sections.title: Transport, Discovery and Lifetime Rules
sections.content:
If no RESTCONF session exists, the subscriber starts a new one. The subscriber MUST run HTTP over TLS (RFC 8446) so content is secure in transit. HTTP sessions alone do not notice quickly when the path to the publisher is lost. Where fast detection is needed, the subscriber SHOULD use a TLS heartbeat (RFC 6520) from subscriber to publisher. Loss of the heartbeat MUST tear down any subscription-related TCP sessions between those endpoints, and the subscriber can then try to re-establish the subscription.

Subscribers learn the supported event streams by querying the streams container of ietf-subscribed-notifications.yang. They learn the supported datastores by following Section 2 of RFC 8527.

A publisher MUST terminate a subscription when it receives a delete-subscription or kill-subscription RPC for it, or when the TLS heartbeat is lost. It MAY terminate a subscription at any time.
sections.plainLanguage: The connection must be locked and private. If the line goes quiet, both sides hang up the subscription, and you can sign up again.

sections.title: Errors and HTTP Status Codes
sections.content:
A successful RPC from RFC 8639 or RFC 8641 gets HTTP status 200. When a request fails, the reply MUST carry an rpc-error element with an error-type of application, an error-tag chosen to match the error identity, and an error-app-tag naming the identity in the form modulename:identityname, for example ietf-subscribed-notifications:no-such-subscription.

The RFC gives tables mapping each error identity to an error-tag and an HTTP code. For example, dscp-unavailable maps to invalid-value and 400, no-such-subscription to invalid-value and 404, insufficient-resources to resource-denied and 409, and replay-unsupported to operation-not-supported and 501. Datastore-specific identities such as unchanging-selection map to operation-failed and 500.

Failed establish-subscription and modify-subscription requests may also carry an error-info node with hints for parameters that might work next time. That yang-data SHOULD NOT include the optional reason leaf, since the error-app-tag already says it.
sections.plainLanguage: When a request fails, the device answers with a number and a short label saying what went wrong, and sometimes a hint on what to try instead.

sections.title: Rules for Modifying, Deleting and Prioritising
sections.content:
Subscription state notifications, such as subscription-modified, MUST be sent in the separate SSE stream of the subscription they refer to. RPCs MUST NOT use the connection that currently delivers that subscription's notifications. For modify-subscription, besides the RPC response on (a), a subscription-modified notification MUST be sent on (b), so the receiver knows exactly where in the stream the new terms took effect.

The RPCs modify-subscription, resync-subscription and delete-subscription SHOULD only be allowed for the same RESTCONF username that invoked establish-subscription, which preserves users' privacy. Administrators may be an exception. kill-subscription can be invoked by any user with the required administrative permissions.

For QoS, if HTTP/2 is used the publisher MUST copy the weighting leaf into the HTTP/2 stream weight, use the parent subscription's HTTP/2 stream as the stream dependency for any dependency, and set the exclusive flag to 0. Subscriptions with the same DSCP value to one publisher should share an HTTP/2 session, and a subscriber cannot use a common session for subscriptions with different DSCP values.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the person who signed up can change or cancel their subscription, unless an administrator steps in. Important feeds can be given a bigger share of the line.

sections.title: The YANG Module and Notification Encoding
sections.content:
Notification messages over RESTCONF are encoded as in Section 6.4 of RFC 8040. The module ietf-restconf-subscribed-notifications (prefix rsn) is very small: one read-only leaf, uri, of type inet:uri, that augments three nodes of RFC 8639. These are the output of establish-subscription, each entry in subscriptions/subscription, and the subscription-modified notification.

Appendix A is non-normative. It mirrors the NETCONF examples of RFC 8640 in JSON, covering establishing, modifying and deleting subscriptions, the state notifications, and an XPath filter example based on VRRP protocol events.
sections.plainLanguage: The only new thing is a single label that holds the special address of your subscription, added in the three places where it is useful.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mandatory-to-implement secure transport for RESTCONF is TLS, and for NETCONF it is SSH. The Network Configuration Access Control Model (RFC 8341) can restrict users to a subset of operations and content.

The new uri leaf may be sensitive, because it shows where subscribed resources might be on a publisher. Only the same user credentials that invoked establish-subscription should be able to access it. The URI is implementation specific and protected by TLS, so even a guessed URI is useless without a username with the required permissions, but it is recommended that URI values not be easily predictable.

A buggy or compromised subscriber could send many establish-subscription requests and use up system resources. The publisher MAY then suspend or terminate some of that subscriber's subscriptions to protect the rest.
sections.plainLanguage: The special address should be hard to guess and only usable by whoever signed up. If someone signs up too many times, the device may cancel some.

messages.note: Sent on a separate connection (b); starts the flow.

messages.label: SSE subscription-modified
messages.note: Required on (b) in addition to the RPC response.
